Wyszkow Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Wyszków, Poland

Demolished. Wyszków, granted town rights in 1502 under the Płock bishops, formally barred Jewish residence for centuries; by 1820, though, 229 Jews made up 30% of the town, achieving communal autonomy by 1858 when they made up 67% of residents. By 1939, 5,000 Jews (42%) lived in Wyszków. Before this cemetery's establishment in the 1820s, local Jews had to bury their dead through whichever neighboring kehilla held jurisdiction at the time - first Węgrów, later Ostrów Mazowiecki, Nasielsk, or Maków Mazowiecki, depending on shifting borders after Poland's partitions. The cemetery, enclosed with a brick wall in the interwar period, was completely devastated during WWII; postwar, the land became farmland, pasture, a sand mine, and partial housing development. Starting in the 1990s, recovered matzevot found around the city were gathered into a 1997 lapidarium wall containing over 120 fragments, the oldest dating to the 1860s.
